qwen.ref_text: On the battlefield, four players with monster-like strength appeared. Each of the players had already destroyed their colonies. These players were so equally strong, they created a four-way deadlock.

lines: Lecture two. Data models and NoSQL. The shape of your data decides how to store it.
One profile page needs data from six tables.
One profile page needs six tables.
So the page asks each table in turn, one lookup at a time.
The page asks each table in turn.
That makes six reads, and a shared key, a foreign key, joins the pieces.
Six reads, joined by a foreign key.
A document keeps the same profile in one place.
A document keeps it all together.
So one read gets the whole page.
One read gets the whole page.
Four hundred profiles all mention the same company.
One company, many profiles.
With tables, the name is stored once, so a rename changes one row.
Tables: change one row.
With documents, every profile holds its own copy, so all four hundred are rewritten.
Documents: rewrite all 400 copies.
If the rewrite misses one, that profile shows the old name.
Miss one and that profile is stale.
Documents can keep old and new shapes side by side.
Old and new shapes sit together.
The app just splits an old name when it reads it.
The app splits old names as it reads.
A table has one shape, so every row must be changed first.
A table must change every row first.
With a million rows, that takes a long time.
With a million rows that takes a long time.
Only then is the table ready.
Only then is the table ready.
Now the page needs the whole profile.
The page wants the whole profile.
From the document, that is one read.
One read from the document.
From the tables, it is six.
Six from the tables.
Now the page needs only the name.
Now it wants only the name.
The document still loads whole, twenty kilobytes for one small name.
A document loads whole: 20 KB for a sliver.
A graph stores things, called vertices, and the links between them, called edges.
A graph stores things and their links.
Each kind of link has a label, such as friend, lives in or works at.
Each kind of link has a label.
Each vertex lists its links in and out. Ben has one coming in, and two going out.
A vertex lists its links in and out.
To find a route, we walk along the edges.
To find a route, walk the edges.
Ana reaches Dee in three hops.
Three hops.
Here are five people, linked in a chain of friends.
Five people, linked in a chain.
In tables, each step is a join. In documents, a fetch. In a graph, a follow.
A join, a fetch, or a follow.
Friends of friends is two hops. Ana reaches Cy.
Two hops: friends of friends.
Now go on to a fourth hop.
Now add a fourth hop.
Tables and documents need one more block for each hop. The graph repeats the same move.
Queries grow, the graph walk does not.
NoSQL means simple design, scaling out, and staying available.
NoSQL: simple, scales out, stays available.
A document store keeps the whole recipe in one place.
Document: the whole recipe.
In a key-value store, the partition key groups items, and the sort key puts them in order.
A partition key groups, a sort key orders.
In a wide-column store, each row keeps its own columns.
Wide-column: columns vary per row.
A graph store keeps things and labelled links.
Graph: things and labelled links.
Follow the links, and Pancakes and Waffles share Flour.
Pancakes and Waffles share Flour.
Here are four jobs, and four families.
Four jobs, four families.
A shopping cart, found by user id, fits key-value.
A cart by user id: key-value.
A whole product page fits a document.
A whole product page: document.
Friends of friends fits a graph.
Friends of friends: graph.
Events with varying columns fit wide-column.
Varying columns: wide-column.
Each job finds its family. Pick by the shape of the question.
Each job finds its family.
If the data is a tree, use a document. If it is shared, use tables.
When the links are the data, use a graph.
Pick one of the four NoSQL families by the question you ask.
